title: A single cell without a brain can solve a maze.
hook: It can also build railway-like networks and use slime as a record of where it has been.

image.alt: Bright yellow Physarum polycephalum plasmodium spreading over dark tree bark.

levels.title: This entire moving network is one cell.

objects.title: A living network on a log

image.alt: Yellow branching slime-mould plasmodium growing across dark bark.

objects.caption: Physarum polycephalum is neither a mushroom nor an animal. Its yellow, many-nucleated plasmodium can spread into a visible web.

objects.title: It pumps information through its own body
objects.text: The feeding stage of Physarum is a giant cell containing many nuclei but no neurons. Its tubes rhythmically contract, driving cytoplasm back and forth. These flows move nutrients and chemical signals; changes in contraction and tube width help coordinate a body that has no central controller.

objects.title: The shortest surviving connection won
objects.text: Toshiyuki Nakagaki and colleagues let Physarum occupy a maze, then placed food at two positions. The organism withdrew from dead ends and maintained a short connection between the food sites. It did not plan a route first: its spreading and pruning produced the result.

objects.title: Oat flakes stood in for cities
objects.text: In 2010 researchers arranged food sources to represent cities around Tokyo. Physarum grew a transport network whose efficiency, cost and resilience compared surprisingly well with the actual rail system. It did not reproduce every line or design a railway deliberately; local growth rules produced similar trade-offs.

sources.title: Rules for biologically inspired adaptive network design

objects.title: Busy tubes become stronger routes
objects.text: Contraction waves push fluid and signals through Physarum's tubes. Models and experiments show how greater flow can reinforce a tube while little-used branches shrink. Repeating this feedback across a network can balance short connections with alternative routes, without any part knowing the whole map.

levels.title: It leaves its memory outside its body.

objects.title: A slime trail marks explored territory
objects.text: As Physarum moves, it deposits extracellular slime. It tends to avoid areas coated with that material, effectively using the environment as a record of where it has already travelled. This is an external spatial memory, not recollection stored in a brain.

sources.title: Slime mold uses an externalized spatial ‘memory’ to navigate in complex environments
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2012

objects.title: 96% escaped a trap when their trails were informative
objects.text: Researchers put food behind a U-shaped barrier. On clean agar, 23 of 24 organisms reached it within 120 hours. On agar already coated with slime, only 8 of 24 succeeded. When everything smelled previously visited, their external memory stopped helping them distinguish new ground.

sources.title: Slime mold uses an externalized spatial ‘memory’ to navigate in complex environments
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2012

levels.title: It can learn—and pass a lesson to another cell.

objects.title: Repeated bitterness became less alarming
objects.text: In 2016, scientists repeatedly made Physarum cross bridges containing repellent quinine or caffeine to reach food. Over several days it crossed more readily. Its aversion returned after a break, and it still reacted to a different repellent: evidence of habituation rather than simple exhaustion.

sources.title: Habituation in non-neural organisms: evidence from slime moulds
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2016

objects.title: Two cells fuse; one acquires the other's learned response
objects.publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2016
objects.description: Researchers fused habituated Physarum with individuals that had never encountered the repellent. After sufficient contact, the previously naive slime mould showed the less-avoidant response—even after separation. What physical or chemical information carries this learned change remains unresolved.

levels.title: It slowed down before the next shock arrived.

objects.title: Three regular shocks produced a fourth response
objects.text: In 2008, researchers gave Physarum three bouts of unfavourable conditions at regular intervals. Each time, it slowed. After conditions returned to normal, some organisms slowed again around the time the next bout would have occurred—even though nothing unpleasant happened then.

objects.title: A timing response is not proof of conscious prediction
objects.description: Saigusa and colleagues analysed how an internal dynamical system could retain traces of periodic stimulation. The experiment demonstrates a time-linked behavioural response; it does not show that a slime mould imagines the future. Even a cell with no neurons can exhibit a kind of temporal memory.
